https://www.radiox.co.uk/artists/the-cur.text: Robert Smith wrote a heartfelt song that became one of his band’s most popular tracks. Here’s how it happened. Adele covered it. Good Charlotte have covered it. Death Cab For Cutie have had a crack at it. Lovesong by The Cure was the second single from the classic Disintegration album to be released in the UK… and it became their biggest ever hit in the United States. The meaning of the song has travelled a long way… and it all began with a simple declaration of devotion. Robert Smith married his long-term girlfriend Mary Poole in the summer of 1988. The pair had met at school when the frontman was just 14 and remained together as Smith became the iconic frontman of The Cure. The Smiths married when the band were enjoying some downtime during work on the album Disintegration. Writing lyrics for the new material, Smith looked to the immediate world around him: he was about to turn 30; a fire at the studio made him worry about losing the photos in his wallet (leading to Pictures Of You) and the prospect of settling down and growing old weighed on his mind.But it was Lovesong that had probably the simplest, yet most personal lyrics on the album. With a chorus that goes “However far away / I will always love you”, it’s Smith’s straightforward dedication to his wife. “I gave Mary a tape of it for a wedding present,” Robert told Select magazine in August 1991. “She went away to the other room to listen to it, then smothered me with kisses. “It’s the most upfront, true, frank and honest thing I’ve ever sung. It’s about love, but also the inability to ever really know someone.” The track was accompanied by another video from The Cure’s long-term visual collaborator Tim Pope, which sees the band performing the song in a dark cave among the stalagmites and stalactites - but Smith was unhappy with the final product.He complained: “The idea was of a fairy cave going on forever, but it looked very cramped and posed. The opening shot is terrible, this lingering shot of a huge phallus that makes no pretensions to be a stalagmite at all.” Released as a single on Monday 21st August 1989, Lovesong spent seven weeks on the UK charts, peaking at Number 18. But it was the USA that took Lovesong to its heart. The single was issued in the States just as The Cure began the North American leg of The Prayer Tour, which included huge stadium shows at Giants Stadium in New Jersey and Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles. The Cure had crossed over from the “alternative” charts into the mainstream and Lovesong was an accessible entry point into the band's extensive back catalogue. This was apparent when Lovesong slowly crept up the Billboard Hot 100 until it peaked at Number 2 in the week ending 21 October. Janet Jackson’s Miss You Much kept it off the top spot and ironically both Jackson and The Cure performed at the 2019 Glastonbury festival. Wonder if they met backstage?“I have to admit that I was actually a bit upset that it stopped at No 2,” Smith later wrote in the sleevenotes to The Cure’s Join The Dots compilation in 2004. “I never got to see what I would really have done with a No 1 single!” Actually, Lovesong DID get to No 1… in Poland, in September 1989. Smith’s comments on that aren’t recorded.While Lovesong still had a proud place in The Cure’s setlist, Adele gave the track a new lease of life when she covered it on her 2011 album 21, where it sits before the epic Someone Like You. This time, Lovesong DID hit the top spot in the US: 21 made the No 1 position in the Billboard 200 album charts in March 2011. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: ‘Yellow 2120’ inside a crawlspace under a home in Altadena, California, on 1 Dec 2025. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP View image in fullscreen ‘Yellow 2120’ inside a crawlspace under a home in Altadena, California, on 1 Dec 2025. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP Los Angeles ‘Cute but unbearable’ freeloading bear discovered in another LA crawlspace ‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces but he just keeps coming back Cecilia Nowell Tue 29 Sep 2026 16.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google He’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering the Los Angeles neighborhood again after he moved in and out of the crawlspace of another home. “Yellow 2120”, as the black bear has been tagged, was spotted in the crawlspace of a home on Minoru Drive on Monday. Steve Clark, whose in-laws live in the house, told NBC LA that they monitored their new neighbor through security cameras, and tried to scare him away by playing loud music and turning on a leaf blower. Bear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LA Read more “I didn’t even realize that the bear could get all the way back to that access point. He has to rip out ductwork and do a bunch of damage to get there,” Clark said. Although those attempts to oust “Yellow 2120” from his adopted den failed, the bear later left on his own. While the homeowners have sealed up their crawlspace, their neighbors are on alert in case the bear decides to move in with them next. “Yellow 2120” made headlines last year when he took up residence under another Altadena home for two months. In November 2025, homeowner Ken Johnson noticed the bear leaving the crawlspace and later contacted California’s department of fish and wildlife for assistance removing it from under his home. Despite sweet-scented lures and ammonia-doused towels, “Yellow 2120” remained in place until January – when Johnson sought assistance from members of the Bear League, a volunteer organization that aims to help humans live in “harmony” with the animals, that was able to force the bear out with paintball guns. “He’s a nuisance and he’s living under my house rent-free,” Johnson told the Orange County Register at the time. “We call him … unbearable, but he’s so cute. Once he gets out, we’ll call him bearable, but for now it’s unbearable.” After the Eaton wildfire tore through the Angeles national forest and scorched parts of Altadena in January 2025, wildlife – including several bears – sought shelter in the community. In the weeks following the fire, at least two 500-plus-pound black bears sought refuge in homes evacuated during the wildfire. Although it’s unclear whether “Yellow 2120” was one of them, he had previously taken up residence under another Altadena home, said Cort Klopping, a fish and wildlife spokesperson. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion As cities encroach closer on bear habitats, bear sightings are growing more common . In 2017, California registered 28 bear sightings in Los Angeles county. In 2023, that number rose to 455. This month Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, told the Guardian that human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation feeding period. This year is on track to be record setting when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said. Black bears – the only species of bear living in California – are largely non-confrontational, having killed only one person in the state in recorded history. The population is estimated to be between 49,000 and 71,000 , with 50% living in the north coast and Cascade regions, and 40% in the Sierra Nevada. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-budge.text: LONDON — John Healey wants to keep his debut budget low-key — but he's also got to show the British public his boss really does feel their pain. The chancellor delivers the first financial statement of the Andy Burnham era Wednesday. The pitch? "Breathing space for today" mixed with some "fresh hope for the future." But with war in Iran driving up costs worldwide, government borrowing at its highest level in a year, and businesses warning they're taxed to the max, Healey is up against it. Advertisement Advertisement Here's how POLITICO's team of reporters will be poring over the big fiscal moment, unveiled at 12.30 p.m. U.K. time Wednesday. U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom I’ll flip straight to the big table two-thirds of the way through the 'red book,' where Treasury officials list the total tax rises and spending cuts, and then the “headroom” against Healey’s fiscal rules in the executive summary. The briefing suggests these numbers will be smaller than the £26 billion in tax rises and £23.6 billion in headroom former Chancellor Rachel Reeves notched up in March this year. The Treasury has turned this into its comms strategy, pointing to “everyday fixes” and non-tax measures like scrapping business red tape. But these numbers will also show how Donald Trump’s war in Iran has reined in Burnham’s ambitions. And they are indicative of something else — the budget just isn’t the main event this time. In the next seven weeks or so we’re expecting [former minister] Alan Milburn’s review of the benefit system, a U.K.-EU summit, a “10-year plan” and a white paper on “rewiring the state.” Then next year is the spending review. That’s when the really hard choices will come — and the budget will give us a sign of how hard, since it will map out a path for departmental spending over the next few years. Advertisement Advertisement U.K. Political Correspondent Sam Blewett Andy Burnham’s team has been speaking a lot about “everyday fixes” — cheapo policies that can rectify real-life niggles. Headphone dodgers? You’re fined . Being ripped off by parking fines? We’ve got your backs . Balking at the cost of the supermarket shop? Gone are the tariffs on your gherkins . That will buy the government a fair amount of goodwill, building a sense that the government isn’t entirely a useless beast being buffeted by global horror shows. But it’ll only go so far. Burnham departs Downing Street in London for prime minister's questions on Oct. 21, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images Healey is under pressure to show bold action on what really matters too — actual interventions that bring down the cost of living. We know already there will be support for household energy bills, a fuel duty freeze, support for pensioners and a hike to the minimum wage. All eyes will be on whether Healey has any more surprises on this front. As costly as any support is for the exchequer, will it all pale in comparison to the effects of the Strait of Hormuz-sealing war with Iran? This is a self-declared “cost of living government” after all. First, I’ll scour watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts to see where the semi-official number crunchers reckon real household disposable income is headed. Then the analysts at the Institute for Fiscal Studies and the Resolution Foundation will provide more insight. Advertisement Advertisement After that, the voices that really matter will be those sitting down to ever-costlier dinner, nursing pricy pints and rolling their eyes at the petrol pumps. Will this budget give Brits enough reason to believe Burnham's new government is a force for good, trying to ease the pain? Or will they deem the new-look administration just the same old ineffective bureaucrats who need sweeping away in favor of a more radical response? Senior Foreign Correspondent Esther Webber and U.K. Defense Reporter Mason Boycott-Owen The number one thing we'll be looking out for in today's budget is how exactly Healey — who quit as defense secretary in the dying days of Keir Starmer's government over exactly this issue — tries to demonstrate he is raising defense spending against a tough backdrop. The chancellor has tried to manage expectations for the Ministry of Defence at the budget pretty closely, initially stating that he would only seek to cover a £4.7 billion pound shortfall in its already-unveiled Defence Investment Plan . In recent weeks, however, the Treasury has suggested he could do more to show the U.K. is moving towards spending 3% of GDP on defense, something Healey sees as an important marker on the way to meeting the NATO target of 3.5%. Media reports leading up to Wednesday suggest an increase will come from money funneled into the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund. But could he have something else in his back pocket? Healey is well aware of the potential for awkward questions about his commitment to follow through on the promises he made just four months ago that he said were crucial to U.K. security, now that he's in charge of the money. Advertisement Advertisement Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers A hike in bank taxes is all but inevitable in today’s budget – but the City of London will be nervously watching how high the increase goes. Along with the lenders, I’ll be looking out for how much taxes are raised, whether any changes are temporary, and whether the City — Britain's financial powerhouse — gets anything in return. The easiest move for Healey is to increase the surcharge banks pay on top of corporation tax. That currently stands at 3%, after Conservative Chancellor Jeremy Hunt reduced it from 8% in 2023 to account for higher corporation taxes. Healey could simply reverse the surcharge to 8%, which would be unpopular with the banks and might not even go far enough for campaigners: the Trades Union Congress has called for an increase to 16%. I’ll also be closely watching for how the bond markets react to the first budget under Burnham. Despite the prime minister describing Britain as “in hock” to the bond markets before he took office, odds are on for a “boring” budget, without any huge spending commitments that might spike borrowing costs. People view the City of London from Parliament Hill on Jan. 3, 2025. | Benjamin Cremel/AFP via Getty Images But any cautious policy changes designed to placate the bond market will have to be tempered alongside demands from the Labour Party. It’s a tricky balance, and Labour MPs showed under Keir Starmer that they were willing to rebel when it mattered. Senior U.K. Energy Correspondent Charlie Cooper A sharp, painful spike in energy bills is coming for Britain; at this budget we’ll find out how much power Healey and Burnham have to help. The latest energy price cap forecasts are brutal. Energy firms expect average, annual household bills to rise by more than £450 in January. They could go even higher in April. Why? Mainly because of gas. The fallout from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has sent wholesale prices soaring to levels not seen since December 2022. Advertisement Advertisement Healey knows how bleak things look, but he may not have the fiscal firepower to offer much help. Burnham has hinted at removing gas standing charges from bills, which could save an average household a modest £27, according to one estimate . Meanwhile, payments to around 6 million low-income households — the Warm Homes Discount — are likely to get a top-up of between £100 and £150. Businesses, meanwhile, could get details of a 10-year plan to bring their energy costs into line with European competitors, according to two people familiar with budget preparations. But with the cost of living and cost of doing business set to rise so high, will that be it? There’s “strong awareness” inside government “of how bad it will get,” said one senior government official. Unfortunately, they added, there are “not the pockets deep enough to do all the things we might like to do.” Elsewhere, we’ll be watching closely to see whether net zero schemes — like the rollout of electric heat pumps — could face cuts to cover shortfalls in defense spending. Technology Reporter Joseph Bambridge Healey put AI and innovation at the heart of his growth plan in a pre-budget speech back in September. Advertisement In that vein, the government has trailed a £600 million spending package to protect the U.K. from AI risks while growing its own share of the sector, calling it a “distinctively British” approach to mitigating risks from the technology while capturing the benefits. The question now is whether more measures to support the U.K.’s tech and AI sector will come on Wednesday, with trade groups calling for bold moves to lower energy costs, tackle energy and planning delays, and help firms invest in AI and upskill workers. Startups are also hoping for tax relief and further reforms to regulation and procurement rules. A relief for founders who re-invest their earnings in the U.K. has been a particular demand from the startup community, which has already bagged a win after Healey ruled out raising capital gains tax. Trade groups are calling for bold moves to lower energy costs, tackle energy and planning delays, and help firms invest in AI and upskill workers. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images AI is also likely to play a significant role in the government’s plans to make Whitehall more efficient, as it did under Reeves. The sector is also closely watching how the chancellor plans to meet his defense spending targets, in the hopes that drone makers and military tech firms might benefit from the uplift. Trade Reporter Caroline Hug I'm looking out for the chancellor's VAT crackdown on foreign sellers, who register as U.K. based companies to avoid paying the tax. Healey is expected to make online marketplaces like Amazon, eBay and Temu responsible for collecting tax owed by all retailers. We're also waiting to see whether the government has more information on its de minimis crackdown, including whether it will introduce a handling fee for small packages below £135. The EU already has one in place. Finally, we'll be looking out for any more detail on the government's suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food, drink, fuel and fertilizer products. Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: A Border Force ship on it way to collect migrant men, women and children in the Channel. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A Border Force ship on it way to collect migrant men, women and children in the Channel. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Immigration and asylum Asylum seekers still being sent to France under ‘one in one out’ weeks after scheme ended Guardian understands Home Office continues to detain dozens of people, with one group forcibly removed this week Diane Taylor Sun 1 Nov 2026 04.00 EST Last modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 04.28 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Home Office is still putting asylum seekers on to planes to France weeks after the controversial scheme to remove them ended, the Guardian has learned. The “one in, one out” scheme was announced by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the former prime minister Keir Starmer in July 2025. It aimed to deter small boats crossing the Channel to the UK from northern France , with some asylum seekers arriving here forcibly returned to France while a similar number in northern France were brought legally to the UK. The scheme ended on 1 October, but the Home Office is understood to still be detaining dozens of people. Officials chartered a plane to France on Wednesday for a group of people who are thought to have arrived on small boats in the UK before the scheme ended. A second flight is scheduled for 17 November. Home Office sources said returns of the remainder of the “one in, one out” cohort were continuing after the deal had ended. According to freedom of information data, almost one-third of the scheme’s deportation flights – seven out of 23 – were cancelled between July and September this year, more than double the total of cancelled deportation flights to France in the first six months of 2026. Emma Ginn, the director of Medical Justice, said that asylum seekers are still being held in detention centres in preparation for forced removal to France. “Even though the scheme has been abandoned, vulnerable people still held under its powers continue to suffer immensely due to the severe harm known to be caused by immigration detention being compounded by the prospect of imminent return to France, where many have reported experiencing violence and abuse at the hands of smugglers.” The scheme has been controversial because it does not appear to have had the intended deterrent effect on small boat crossings, and many asylum seekers have reported being left homeless or abused by smugglers. Some were told they would be sent back to other EU countries they passed through on their journeys to the UK. While small boat crossings have reduced by approximately 40% so far this year compared with the same period last year, there has been a similar level of reduction in irregular migration to Europe over the same period. Home Office data showed that after no crossings for three weeks, 263 people crossed in three boats on Thursday and 671 people in nine boats on Friday. The Guardian understands that at least seven asylum seekers returned to France have come back to the UK since 1 October, with reports of several more waiting in northern France to cross back to the UK in the next few days when a favourable weather window is forecast. View image in fullscreen The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, during a presentation of resources used to counter illegal immigration in April 2026. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/AFP/Getty Images The Guardian has interviewed two asylum seekers who the UK sent to France during the scheme who have returned to UK since 1 October and are having their asylum claims processed in the UK. The first is Syrian and the second Iranian. Both returned just days after one in, one out finished. “At first the Home Office put me back in detention,” said the Syrian man. “They said they were looking for a safe third country to deport me to. But there wasn’t one, so they released me and my asylum claim is now being looked at in the UK. I am very relieved that I am no longer locked up and am safe in the UK.” The Iranian man said he had been planning to return to the UK for several months as he had been abused by smugglers in France and wanted to escape as soon as he could. “I was tortured and beaten by the smugglers. I was too afraid to go outside in France. People have no idea how difficult the life is in France for people like us sent back by the UK.” Maddie Harris of Humans for Rights Network questioned the purpose of the scheme as hundreds gather along the French coast waiting to cross the Channel. “Hundreds of millions of pounds of British taxpayers’ money has been transferred to the French government. Men, women and children are teargassed and beaten on the beaches, after being subjected to repetitive, violent evictions from living sites, yet people still cross to the UK. This money has done nothing but cause harm. Our government fails to acknowledge the most obvious policy to prevent dangerous crossings: accessible safe routes for all to claim asylum in the UK.” According to evidence the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, gave to a recent session of parliament’s cross-party home affairs committee, removing people to France has cost at least £78m. Some who were sent to France returned to UK and were then returned to France a second time, incurring a further cost. View image in fullscreen Migrants look on as police clear a camp in Dunkirk. Photograph: Ed Ram/The Guardian One asylum seeker who was sent back to France under the scheme and is now in the area known as the “Jungle” in Dunkirk, a camp where asylum seekers pitch tents while waiting to cross the Channel, told the Guardian: “There are at least five or six people from one in, one out waiting in the Jungle at the moment to cross the Channel back to the UK. The place is so full at the moment of people waiting to cross there is no space for people to lie down and sleep. The Home Office has not stopped people reaching the UK, but both the smugglers and the French government have made a lot of money out of this scheme.” Another, who said he was 17 years old, explained he had been caught by police when trying to board a lorry to cross the Channel a few days ago but would continue to try to reach the UK. “It is very dangerous to get here but we have no choice. Somehow we will handle it.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum France Europe Home Office Migration Refugees news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
